transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 | Start: 10:00 AM PDT | Duration: ~56m
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Celadon Head of Cloud), Tomás Rivera (CTO), Lily Huang (Platform Eng), Erica Jones (Procurement)

Summary:
Brief partner/discovery call with Celadon Network (cloud + reseller of GPU capacity) to align on capacity routing, private vs hosted deployment tradeoffs, security requirements and pilot scope. Goal: determine feasibility of a reserved capacity pilot with VPC peering and routing policies, and identify technical owners for benchmark.

Topics covered:
- Capacity mapping and routing policies (latency vs cost tiers)
- VPC/Private deployment options (peering vs on-prem appliance)
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML
- Benchmarks: sequence lengths, batching, quantization impact, KV cache behavior
- Commercial: committed capacity vs burst pricing, PO timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lena from Redwood, account lead. We got about an hour, rough agenda is partner alignment on capacity and routing, security checks, and then next steps for a pilot. Marco and Priya are on for technical questions. Samir, do you want to kick off with a quick run-through of Celadon?
[00:12] Samir Patel: Yeah sure, thanks. So, Celadon we run a cloud reseller model, we sell GPU capacity in three regions north-amer, eu-west, apac. Mostly customers are enterprise SaaS that want dedicated bursts of GPUs. We're exploring a closer integration to offer Redwood-powered inference as a managed option. Key thing for us is predictable latency for tiered SKUs and clean billing.
[00:30] Tomás Rivera: And from our platform side we care about routing. We want to route low-latency customers to dedicated pools and cheaper inference to shared hosted models, ideally automatic.
[00:44] Marco Ruiz: Right. That's a common pattern. Redwood supports policy-based routing — you can route by SLA, cost, region, customer tag, etc. There are a couple ways to accomplish it: one is Hosted API with smart routing rules, the other is Redwood Dedicated deployed in your region and we route to it when a request matches a policy.
[00:58] Lily Huang: When you say "Dedicated" are we talking about reserved GPU pools that live in our VPC or your managed colo? Clarify please.
[01:06] Priya Anand: Good question. There are two deployment models: Redwood Dedicated is reserved capacity that can be in our cloud region and connect via peering, or Redwood Private which can be deployed in a customer VPC or on-prem if needed. For Celadon as a reseller you'd likely start with Dedicated in your region with VPC peering, and later consider Private for regulated customers.
[01:23] Erica Jones: From procurement, key constraints for us are: we need SOC2 Type II evidence, KMS integration, and audit log retention for 1 year. Also want clarity on how data at rest is encrypted.
[01:34] Lena Park: Understood. We can share SOC2 reports, and our Private offering integrates with customer KMS for key management; hosted also uses our cloud KMS but we can discuss bring-your-own-key for dedicated routes. We'll include a network diagram and the SOC2 artifact in the follow-up.
[01:48] Samir Patel: Great. On technical — Tomás, Lily and I put together a short list of workloads: 1) low-latency chat for 4k token windows, 2) batch embedding jobs (500k vectors/day), 3) a reranker workload with long context. We want to understand per-token cost and expected p99 latency under mixed load.
[02:05] Marco Ruiz: Awesome, that's exactly what we'll benchmark. A couple of notes: for long context workloads we recommend enabling KV caching and an optimized kernel path — sometimes transcribed as "kayvee cache" in notes — that reduces repeated prefix compute. Also quantization choices significantly affect GPU memory and throughput — 4-bit quantized models can give x2 throughput in many cases but vary by model.
[02:26] Tomás Rivera: Do you have a sense of how that interacts with batching? We try to keep latency under 200ms p50 for our chat customers.
[02:33] Marco Ruiz: There's always a trade-off. We use continuous batching where the runtime will hold requests for a few millis to form batches. You can tune max latency SLOs per route. For sub-200ms p50 you usually set smaller batch windows, more dedicated pools per region, and possibly pin to higher-memory GPUs. We'll mock recommended settings after we see your request distribution.
[02:52] Samir Patel: For routing, can Redwood's console surface cost delta per route? We need to show customers price/unit differences between routed tiers.
[03:00] Priya Anand: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route cost and latency breakdown, token-level costs, and we can expose that to Celadon ops via read-only dashboard or API. If you want more granular billing we'll sync on tagging semantics.
[03:12] Lily Huang: On networking — is peering enough or do you also support private link/ingress? Some of our customers insist on private endpoints.
[03:19] Marco Ruiz: We support VPC peering and private link-like patterns for the major clouds. For on-prem or air-gapped we can do Redwood Private as a package. Note some features like our public streaming endpoints are only in hosted unless you configure routing and edge proxies.
[03:34] Tomás Rivera: How intrusive is the Private install? Our infra team prefers minimal changes.
[03:39] Priya Anand: Private can be deployed as a control plane with customer-managed networking. For an initial pilot peering to Dedicated is less invasive. If you go Private later, we provide a deployment playbook; it usually involves a handful of helm charts and a small edge appliance for ingress. We also have a support track for air-gapped installs.
[03:56] Samir Patel: Security question — we need SSO. Do you support SAML/Okta and can we sync our groups to RBAC?
[04:03] Lena Park: Yes, SAML/Okta is supported, and RBAC group sync is available in Redwood Console for dedicated/private. For hosted we have enterprise SSO options. We'll include an SSO matrix in the follow-up.
[04:14] Erica Jones: Also need to know about data separation. If two Celadon customers use the same Dedicated pool, how is tenant isolation enforced?
[04:22] Marco Ruiz: Isolation is at the request-routing and model-instance level. In dedicated pools you can reserve GPUs per tenant, or use namespace isolation inside the runtime. For strict tenancy, we recommend separate pools for each high-security customer. We'll document options with pros/cons.
[04:36] Tomás Rivera: Good. On costs: do you have committed monthly pricing? Our business model needs predictable margins.
[04:43] Lena Park: We offer committed capacity contracts for Dedicated with monthly or annual commits. Pricing varies by GPU class, region, and commitment duration. We also support burst credits to allow short-term spikes. I'll send a tailored pricing spreadsheet after this call.
[04:57] Samir Patel: Perfect. For the benchmark, what access do you need?
[05:02] Marco Ruiz: Ideally: a test VPC peering, a service account with limited access, and a list of representative payloads including token distribution and parallel concurrency. If peering isn't possible, we can run a remote perf harness against a dedicated test endpoint. We'll also want logs and tracing hooks for deeper triage.
[05:20] Lily Huang: We can provision a test subnet and service account. We'll need to check procurement for an MSA/PO to start benchmark tooling access though.
[05:27] Erica Jones: Procurement expects to see a data handling addendum and SOC2 before signing.
[05:31] Lena Park: Understood — we'll include SOC2 and a sample DPA plus the network diagram.
[05:36] Samir Patel: A couple of tricky things: 1) we have customers on mixed GPU types and want automatic model variant fallback if capacity is constrained. 2) We sometimes need token-level inspection for debugging — how intrusive is that from privacy/PII perspective?
[05:49] Marco Ruiz: For fallback we do support automatic model variant routing: you can define compatible model sets and fallback policies. For token inspection, we expose trace hooks and anonymization options; token-level logging is configurable and can be disabled or scrubbed. We integrate with audit logs too.
[06:04] Tomás Rivera: On model variants — does Redwood maintain multiple quantized builds per model and switch at runtime, or is that something we must manage?
[06:10] Priya Anand: We maintain multiple compatible variants for common models and can serve quantized versions when appropriate. However, for some custom models you'll want us to run a quantization pipeline in onboarding. We can include a model-variant matrix for your most common models.
[06:25] Samir Patel: Anything you need from us for a pilot dataflow diagram?
[06:28] Marco Ruiz: A diagram showing ingress route, where you're doing authentication, where peering ends, and representative customer flow is sufficient. If you can annotate expected concurrency and token sizes that helps.
[06:38] Lily Huang: We'll produce that.
[06:40] Tomás Rivera: One more practical question: SLA and monitoring. Do you offer synthetic checks and alerting we can integrate into our pager?
[06:46] Marco Ruiz: Yes Redwood Console can emit alerts, and we have tracing and per-route SLOs. Synthetic monitors can be configured and we can forward alerts to your pager or webhook.
[06:55] Samir Patel: Competitive sanity check: some of our customers consider CloudlyGPU because they price lower. How do you typically position vs who comes in cheaper?
[07:02] Lena Park: We lean on predictable unit economics, observability, and routing flexibility. Price per token isn't the only lever — cost controls like batching/kv cache and quantization recommendations reduce unit cost while keeping latency SLOs. We'll put comparative notes in the spreadsheet.
[07:18] Erica Jones: Procurement also wants to know liability limits and indemnity language. Can legal provide a sample?
[07:23] Lena Park: Yes — we'll include a sample MSA and highlight the insurance/indemnity clauses commonly requested.
[07:30] Priya Anand: Technical note: for long-running rerankers we sometimes recommend offloading embeddings to a vector store to reduce repeated model calls; that can affect architecture and cost.
[07:39] Tomás Rivera: We're already using a managed vector DB, so that should be fine.
[07:42] Samir Patel: For the pilot timeline what are realistic windows? We want to be able to announce a pilot to one key customer in September.
[07:49] Marco Ruiz: For a basic perf pilot: 2 weeks to provision test environment and peering, 1 week to run baseline benchmarks, 1 week to iterate — so 4 weeks total if there's no legal/PO blocker. If procurement slows it can stretch.
[08:02] Lena Park: So timeline action: if Celadon can get PO/MSA started this month we can aim to have pilot infra and first perf runs in early September.
[08:10] Erica Jones: We'll try to accelerate.
[08:13] Samir Patel: Cool. Any gotchas you want to flag for our infra team?
[08:17] Marco Ruiz: A couple: ensure you allow sufficient MTU and make sure flow logs are enabled for debugging; if you're doing VPC peering check routing priorities — sometimes customers accidentally route traffic to a NAT gateway causing latency. Also, if you run quantized builds make sure GPU drivers and CUDA stacks match versions; we can provide a compatibility matrix.
[08:37] Lily Huang: That MTU note is gold — we ran into it previously.
[08:40] Tomás Rivera: For benchmarks can you share a simple harness? We'd prefer to run some workload shapes ourselves before you run remote tests.
[08:47] Marco Ruiz: Yep we'll share a perf harness repo and a short checklist. It includes scripts to generate token distributions and concurrency patterns.
[08:55] Lena Park: Quick recap of next steps before close: 1) Redwood to send capacity/pricing spreadsheet, SOC2, sample DPA/MSA, SSO matrix, and perf harness link. 2) Celadon to share pilot diagram, representative workloads, and procurement timeline. 3) Schedule 2-hour technical deep-dive the week of Aug 10. Sound good?
[09:15] Tomás Rivera: Sounds good.
[09:17] Erica Jones: Yep.
[09:19] Samir Patel: One last thing — do you have an example of committed billing granularity? We want day-level usage export.
[09:26] Priya Anand: We can export daily usage via API or CSV and we support billing tags. We'll include those details.
[09:33] Lena Park: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts later today.
[09:37] Tomás Rivera: Thanks all.
[09:39] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms ("kayvee" for KV), some speaker mis-attribution near crosstalk, overall medium. Shared artifacts: partner-deck link (sent in chat): https://redwood.link/celadon-partner-deck, perf-harness repo: https://github.com/redwood/perf-harness (readme + scripts), sample MSA: https://redwood.link/sample-msa.
